claims.text: The initial magnetic high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous solid solution with few secondary phases.
A controlled post-synthesis annealing treatment can induce fine secondary-phase precipitation.
The annealing treatment can induce precipitates without compromising the overall solid-solution stability.
The annealing-induced precipitates will be nanometer-scale, non-magnetic, and located along grain boundaries.
Annealing slightly below the primary-phase decomposition temperature for 1–4 hours should permit nucleation of secondary phases.
The annealing treatment should be conducted under an inert atmosphere.
Fine grain-boundary precipitates act as magnetic-domain-wall pinning centers.
Pinning by the precipitates makes domain-wall motion more energetically unfavorable.
More difficult domain-wall motion increases the coercive field.
The tailored annealing treatment will increase coercive field by more than 20% relative to a matched untreated baseline.
Untreated baseline alloys have a lower density of grain-boundary precipitates than tailored-annealed alloys.
The lower precipitate density of untreated baseline alloys corresponds to a lower coercive field.
The coercivity-enhancing effect should hold only where the high-entropy phase remains stable.
Unwanted phase segregation or excessive precipitate growth may deteriorate magnetic performance.
